goals: Describe the Geiger–Marsden alpha-scattering experiment, its observations and Rutherford’s conclusions
Calculate the distance of closest approach of an alpha particle and use it to estimate the size of a nucleus
State Bohr’s postulates and derive the radius and speed of the electron in the nth orbit of hydrogen

slides.narration: Everything around us is made of atoms about a ten-billionth of a metre across. How can we find out what is inside something so small? In nineteen hundred and nine, Geiger and Marsden fired fast alpha particles at a very thin gold foil and watched where they went. What they saw overturned the accepted picture of the atom, and led first to Rutherford’s nuclear model and then to Bohr’s theory of hydrogen.

slides.heading: Before the nucleus: Thomson’s model
slides.body_md: J. J. Thomson pictured the atom as a sphere of **positive charge spread evenly** through its volume, with electrons embedded in it, like currants in a bun. A fast, heavy α particle (charge +2e) passing through such an atom meets only weak, spread-out forces.
bullets: Prediction: every α particle goes through a thin foil with a deflection of a small fraction of a degree.
Nothing in the model can turn an α particle back.

rows: Spread through the whole atom, electrons embedded in it
Only tiny deflections; none thrown back
Concentrated in a tiny central nucleus
Mostly straight through; a few large deflections, some thrown back

visual.alt: Table comparing the Thomson and Rutherford models of the atom: where the positive charge is and what each predicts for alpha particles passing through a thin foil

slides.narration: Before nineteen eleven, the favoured model was Thomson’s. The positive charge was thought to be spread evenly through the atom, with electrons dotted through it like currants in a bun. An alpha particle is heavy and fast, and inside such an atom the forces on it are weak and partly cancel. So the model predicted that every alpha particle would pass through a thin foil almost straight.

slides.heading: The Geiger–Marsden experiment
slides.body_md: A narrow beam of fast α particles from a radioactive source in a lead block falls on a **very thin gold foil**. A **zinc sulphide screen** viewed through a **microscope** turns round the foil; each α particle that strikes it makes a tiny flash (scintillation), and the flashes are counted at each scattering angle θ.
bullets: The whole apparatus is **evacuated**, so the α particles are not stopped or scattered by air.
Gold can be beaten very thin, so most α particles meet only one nucleus on the way through.

slides.narration: In the experiment, a radioactive source inside a lead block sends a narrow beam of alpha particles onto a very thin gold foil. A screen coated with zinc sulphide gives a tiny flash of light each time an alpha particle hits it, and an observer counts the flashes through a microscope. The screen and microscope can be turned round the foil to any angle. The chamber is pumped out, so air does not stop the particles.

slides.heading: What they saw
slides.body_md: Counting flashes at different angles gave three results:
bullets: The count falls very steeply as θ increases, but never quite to zero.

rows: Most α particles pass straight through or with tiny deflections
Most of the atom is empty space
A few are deflected through large angles
The positive charge is concentrated in a very small region
About 1 in several thousand bounces back (θ > 90°)
That region holds nearly all the mass: a heavy, tiny nucleus

visual.alt: Table of the three observations of the alpha-scattering experiment and the conclusion drawn from each

slides.narration: The results were startling. Almost all the alpha particles went straight through the foil, or were bent by a degree or two. A few were deflected through large angles. And roughly one in several thousand came back towards the source, as if it had bounced off something. Rutherford said it was as if a shell fired at tissue paper had come back and hit you.

slides.heading: How a tiny nucleus explains it
slides.body_md: Rutherford proposed that the positive charge and nearly all the mass of an atom are concentrated in a **nucleus** about $10^{-14}$ m across, with electrons moving round it at large distances.
bullets: An α particle far from every nucleus is hardly deflected; one aimed close to a nucleus feels a huge Coulomb repulsion and is turned through a large angle.
The electrons are far too light to deflect an α particle (about 1/7300 of its mass).
Only a few α particles happen to be aimed close enough to a nucleus: hence few large deflections.

visual.alt: Computed paths of alpha particles near a gold nucleus

slides.narration: Rutherford explained all three results with a new model. The positive charge and nearly all the mass are packed into a tiny nucleus, with the electrons far outside it. An alpha particle that passes far from every nucleus feels almost no force. One aimed very close to a nucleus is repelled strongly and swings round through a large angle. Because the nucleus is so small, very few particles come that close.

slides.heading: Distance of closest approach
slides.body_md:
An α particle of kinetic energy K aimed **head-on** at a nucleus of charge Ze slows down, stops momentarily and returns. At the turning point all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy (the heavy nucleus is taken as fixed):
$$K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{(2e)(Ze)}{d}\quad\Rightarrow\quad d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2Ze^2}{K}$$
bullets: d is the **distance of closest approach**: the nucleus cannot be larger than d, so d is an upper limit to its radius.
Doubling K halves d.

x.label: distance r from the gold nucleus (fm)

visual.alt: Graph of the electrostatic potential energy of an alpha particle against its distance from a gold nucleus, from 10 to 150 femtometres: the energy rises as one over r; horizontal dashed lines at 5.0 and 8.0 megaelectronvolts meet the curve at 45.5 and 28.4 femtometres, the distances of closest approach for head-on alpha particles of those energies
visual.caption: A head-on α particle stops where U equals its initial kinetic energy: more energy, closer approach.

slides.narration: Now follow an alpha particle aimed straight at a nucleus. As it gets closer, the repulsion slows it down, until for an instant it stops and then turns back. At that moment all of its kinetic energy has been stored as electrostatic potential energy. Equating the two gives the distance of closest approach. Since the particle never touches the nucleus, the nucleus must be smaller than this distance.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how small is a gold nucleus?
slides.body_md: An α particle of kinetic energy 5.0 MeV is aimed head-on at a gold nucleus (Z = 79). Find the distance of closest approach, and compare it with the radius of a gold atom, about 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
bullets: $d = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{8.0 \times 10^{-13}} = 4.55 \times 10^{-14}$ m, about 45.5 fm.
The atom is $\dfrac{1.4 \times 10^{-10}}{4.55 \times 10^{-14}} \approx 3100$ times larger than this upper limit for the nucleus.

x.label: distance r from the gold nucleus (fm)

visual.alt: Graph of the electrostatic potential energy of an alpha particle against its distance from a gold nucleus, from 10 to 150 femtometres: the energy rises as one over r; horizontal dashed lines at 5.0 and 8.0 megaelectronvolts meet the curve at 45.5 and 28.4 femtometres, the distances of closest approach for head-on alpha particles of those energies
visual.caption: A head-on α particle stops where U equals its initial kinetic energy: more energy, closer approach.

slides.narration: Five megaelectronvolts is eight times ten to the minus thirteen joules. Putting the charges of the alpha particle and the gold nucleus into the formula gives a closest approach of about four point five five times ten to the minus fourteen metres, or forty five femtometres. The whole atom is roughly three thousand times bigger. The gold nucleus is even smaller than this, about seven femtometres, as faster particles later showed.

slides.heading: Sizes: atom and nucleus
slides.body_md: Closest-approach estimates and later experiments give nuclear radii of about $10^{-15}$ to $10^{-14}$ m, against $10^{-10}$ m for atoms.
bullets: The nucleus is about 10⁴ to 10⁵ times smaller in radius than the atom, so it fills only about 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom’s volume.
Faster α particles get closer and give smaller (better) upper limits.

rows: Closest approach of 5 MeV α to gold

visual.alt: Table of the sizes of an atom, the closest approach of a 5 megaelectronvolt alpha particle to gold, a nucleus, and the fraction of the atom’s volume taken up by the nucleus

slides.narration: Experiments like this, and later ones with faster particles, show that a nucleus is about ten to the minus fifteen to ten to the minus fourteen metres across, while an atom is about ten to the minus ten metres. If an atom were blown up to the size of a cricket stadium, its nucleus would be a small marble at the centre, yet it would hold almost all the mass.

slides.heading: Where Rutherford’s model fails
slides.body_md: An electron moving in a circle is **accelerated**, and classical electromagnetism says an accelerated charge **radiates** energy. So the electron should:
bullets: Lose energy and **spiral into the nucleus** in about 10⁻⁸ s: atoms would not be stable.
Radiate at a steadily rising frequency, giving a **continuous spectrum**, not the sharp lines observed.

visual.alt: Why a classical Rutherford atom would collapse

slides.narration: Rutherford’s model has a serious flaw. An electron going round in a circle is accelerating towards the centre, and an accelerating charge should send out electromagnetic waves. Losing energy, it would spiral inwards in about a hundred-millionth of a second, radiating at an ever-rising frequency. Atoms would collapse, and they would give out a continuous spread of colours. Real atoms are stable and give sharp lines.

slides.heading: Bohr’s postulates (1913)
slides.body_md: Bohr kept the nucleus and the circular orbits, but added rules for hydrogen:
bullets: **1. Stationary orbits:** the electron moves in certain circular orbits without radiating; the Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force.
**2. Quantum condition:** in an allowed orbit the angular momentum is a whole multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$: $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, n = 1, 2, 3, …
**3. Frequency condition:** radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits: $h\nu = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}$.

slides.narration: In nineteen thirteen, Niels Bohr kept Rutherford’s nucleus but added three rules. First, the electron can move in certain orbits without radiating. Second, in those orbits its angular momentum is a whole number times h over two pi; the whole number n labels the orbit. Third, light is given out or taken in only when the electron jumps from one allowed orbit to another, as a single photon carrying the energy difference.

slides.heading: Radius of the nth orbit
slides.body_md:
Coulomb force = centripetal force, and the quantum condition:
$$\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\quad(1),\qquad mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\quad(2)$$
From (2), $v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi m r}$; put it into (1), $mv^2r = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$:
$$r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 n^2 h^2}{\pi m e^2} = 0.53\,n^2\ \text{Å}$$
bullets: r ∝ n²: radii in the ratio 1 : 4 : 9 : 16 …; r₁ = 0.53 Å is the **Bohr radius**.

slides.narration: Two equations do the work. The electric attraction supplies the centripetal force, and the angular momentum is n h over two pi. From the second, write the speed in terms of the radius and substitute into the first. The radius comes out as epsilon nought n squared h squared over pi m e squared. For hydrogen in its lowest orbit this is about half an angstrom, and it grows as n squared.

slides.heading: Speed of the electron in the nth orbit
slides.body_md:
Divide $mv^2r = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ by $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$:
$$v_n = \dfrac{e^2}{2\varepsilon_0 n h} = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^{6}}{n}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$
bullets: v ∝ 1/n: the electron moves more slowly in the larger outer orbits.
$v_1 \approx \dfrac{c}{137}$: fast, but well below the speed of light.
The orbital frequency $v/2\pi r$ falls as $1/n^3$.

visual.alt: Table of the radius, speed and angular momentum of the electron in the nth Bohr orbit of hydrogen, with expressions and values

slides.narration: Dividing one equation by the other gets rid of the mass and the radius, leaving the speed as e squared over two epsilon nought n h. In the first orbit this is about two point two million metres per second, roughly one hundred and thirty seventh of the speed of light. The speed falls as one over n, so outer electrons move more slowly, and they go round far less often.

slides.body_md: Key results:

Tiny, heavy, positive nucleus; electrons far outside

slides.narration: To sum up: the scattering of alpha particles showed that an atom has a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus. The distance of closest approach of a head-on alpha particle sets an upper limit to its size. Rutherford’s model could not explain why atoms are stable, so Bohr added quantised orbits, with radii growing as n squared and speeds falling as one over n.

slides.narration: Pass the light from a glowing hydrogen tube through a prism and you do not get a rainbow, but a few sharp coloured lines. Beyond the visible, there are more lines in the ultraviolet and the infrared. In this part we use Bohr’s orbits to find the energy of the electron, draw the energy levels of hydrogen, and see how every line comes from a jump between two levels.

slides.heading: Kinetic, potential and total energy
slides.body_md:
From $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$: $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$. The potential energy of the electron (−e) at distance r from the proton (+e) is $U = -\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$. So
$$E = K + U = -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r},\qquad K = -E,\quad U = 2E$$

visual.alt: Table of the kinetic, potential and total energy of the electron in a Bohr orbit, in terms of the radius and of n

slides.narration: The force equation gives the kinetic energy directly: one half m v squared equals e squared over eight pi epsilon nought r. The potential energy of the electron near the proton is negative, and twice as large in size. Adding them, the total energy is minus e squared over eight pi epsilon nought r. So in every orbit the kinetic energy equals minus the total energy, and the potential energy is twice the total.

slides.heading: Energy of the nth orbit
slides.body_md:
Put $r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 n^2 h^2}{\pi m e^2}$ into $E = -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$:
$$E_n = -\dfrac{me^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2 n^2 h^2} = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}\ \text{eV}$$
bullets: As n increases, E increases (becomes less negative) while K decreases.

Putting in the constants, the energy of the nth level is minus thirteen point six electronvolts divided by n squared. The ground state is at minus thirteen point six, the next at minus three point four, and the levels crowd towards zero as n grows.

slides.heading: Why the energy is negative
slides.body_md: Zero energy means the electron is **free and at rest far from the proton** (n → ∞). A negative total energy means the electron is **bound**: energy must be supplied to free it.
bullets: **Ionisation energy** from level n: $+\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$ eV (13.6 eV from the ground state).
**Excitation energy:** the energy to lift the electron from the ground state to a higher level, e.g. 10.2 eV to n = 2.
An electron with E > 0 is free; it can have any energy.

slides.narration: The zero of energy is chosen as the electron at rest, far away from the proton. A bound electron has less energy than that, so its total energy is negative. The more negative, the more tightly it is held. To free an electron from the ground state, we must supply thirteen point six electronvolts, the ionisation energy. Lifting it to a higher level needs a smaller amount, called an excitation energy.

slides.heading: Emission, absorption and the Rydberg formula
slides.body_md:
A jump from $n_2$ down to $n_1$ emits one photon with $h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1} = \dfrac{me^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2h^2}\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$:
$$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right),\qquad R = \dfrac{me^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2ch^3} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$$
bullets: R is the **Rydberg constant**; $1/\lambda$ is the wave number.
Absorption is the reverse jump, upwards, taking in a photon of exactly the same energy.

slides.narration: When the electron drops from a higher level to a lower one, the atom sends out a single photon whose energy equals the difference between the levels. Dividing by h c gives the reciprocal of the wavelength as a constant times one over the lower n squared minus one over the upper n squared. That constant is the Rydberg constant, about one point one times ten to the seven per metre.

slides.heading: The five series
slides.body_md: Lines that end on the same lower level form a **series**:
bullets: Lyman (n₁ = 1) ultraviolet; Balmer (n₁ = 2) visible and near ultraviolet; Paschen (n₁ = 3), Brackett (n₁ = 4) and Pfund (n₁ = 5) infrared.
The jump from n₂ = ∞ gives the **series limit**, the shortest wavelength of the series.

slides.narration: All the jumps that end on the ground state form the Lyman series, in the ultraviolet. Jumps ending on the second level form the Balmer series, whose first lines are visible. Jumps ending on the third, fourth and fifth levels give the Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series, all in the infrared. A jump from infinity gives the series limit, the shortest wavelength in each series.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a violet Balmer line
slides.body_md: Find the wavelength of the line emitted when the electron in hydrogen falls from n = 5 to n = 2. Name its series and region. (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)
bullets: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{25}\right) = 1.097 \times 10^{7} \times 0.21 = 2.304 \times 10^{6}$ m⁻¹.
$\lambda = 4.341 \times 10^{-7}$ m $= 434.1$ nm: Balmer series (ends on n = 2), **visible** (violet).
Check with energies: $E_5 - E_2 = 13.6\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{25}\right) = 2.856$ eV, and $\dfrac{1240}{2.856} = 434$ nm.

visual.alt: Table of the five hydrogen series: the level each ends on, the levels it starts from, its region of the spectrum and its range of wavelengths from the series limit to the first line

slides.narration: One quarter minus one twenty fifth is zero point two one. Multiplying by the Rydberg constant gives about two point three times ten to the six per metre, so the wavelength is about four hundred and thirty four nanometres. The line ends on the second level, so it belongs to the Balmer series, and it is violet light. The energy difference, about two point eight six electronvolts, gives the same answer.

slides.heading: Series limits and overlaps
slides.body_md: Series limit: $\lambda_\infty = \dfrac{n_1^2}{R}$. First (longest) line: $n_2 = n_1 + 1$.
bullets: Lyman 91.2–121.5 nm and Balmer 364.6–656.3 nm do not overlap.
Paschen (820–1875 nm), Brackett (1459–4051 nm) and Pfund (2279–7458 nm) overlap: a line’s wavelength alone may fit two series, so check with the formula.
Only Balmer lines from n₂ = 3 to 6 are visible (656, 486, 434, 410 nm); from n₂ = 7 on they are ultraviolet.

slides.narration: First decide the series. Twelve hundred and eighty two nanometres is too long for the Balmer series and too short for any Brackett line, so it must be a Paschen line, ending on level three. Then solve the Rydberg formula for the upper level: one over n squared comes out as nought point nought four, so n is five. The line comes from the jump from five to three.

slides.heading: How many lines?
slides.body_md:
Atoms excited to level n can return by many routes. The number of different lines possible is
$$N = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$$
bullets: A single atom emits only one photon per jump; a gas of many atoms shows all the lines together.
Cool hydrogen is almost entirely in n = 1, so its **absorption** spectrum shows only Lyman lines.

slides.narration: If many atoms are excited to the fourth level, some jump straight down to the ground state while others stop at the third or second level on the way. Every pair of levels gives a different line, so the number of possible lines is n times n minus one over two, six for the fourth level. Cool hydrogen absorbs only from the ground state, so its absorption spectrum shows just the Lyman lines.

slides.heading: Finding R from the Balmer lines
slides.body_md: For the Balmer series, $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{R}{4} - \dfrac{R}{n^2}$: a graph of $1/\lambda$ against $1/n^2$ is a **straight line** of slope $-R$ and intercept $R/4$ (the series limit).
bullets: Measured Balmer wavelengths fall on this line, which is how the Rydberg constant was first found from experiment.

visual.alt: Graph of the reciprocal of wavelength against one over n squared for the Balmer lines from n equals 3 to 6: the points lie on a straight line of slope minus R, the Rydberg constant; the intercept at one over n squared equal to zero is R over 4, the series limit at 364.6 nanometres
visual.caption: A straight line of slope −R: the Balmer wavelengths give the Rydberg constant.

slides.narration: The Rydberg formula can be tested with a graph. For the Balmer lines, plot one over the wavelength against one over n squared for the upper level. The points fall on a straight line. Its slope is minus the Rydberg constant, and where it meets the axis at one over n squared equal to zero, it gives the series limit. Measured wavelengths agree with Bohr’s value of R.

slides.heading: Successes and limits of Bohr’s model
slides.body_md: Bohr’s model explains the stability of hydrogen, its size (0.53 Å), its ionisation energy (13.6 eV) and every wavelength of its spectrum. But:
bullets: It works only for hydrogen and one-electron ions; it cannot handle electron–electron repulsion in atoms like helium.
It cannot explain the relative intensities of the lines, or why some lines split into close pairs (fine structure).
It mixes classical orbits with quantum rules without explaining them; quantum mechanics replaces sharp orbits with probability clouds.

visual.alt: Table of what Bohr’s model explains and what it cannot explain

slides.narration: Bohr’s model was a triumph for hydrogen. It gave the right size of the atom, the right ionisation energy and every wavelength of the spectrum. But it fails for atoms with two or more electrons, because it ignores the repulsion between them. It cannot say why some lines are brighter than others. And its rules were simply assumed; later, quantum mechanics replaced its sharp orbits with clouds of probability.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 2
slides.body_md: Key results for hydrogen:

rows: Electron bound; 13.6/n² eV needed to free it
n₁ = 1 Lyman (UV), 2 Balmer (visible), 3 Paschen, 4 Brackett, 5 Pfund (IR)

visual.alt: Summary table of the energies of the Bohr atom, the meaning of negative energy, the photon condition, the Rydberg formula and the five series

slides.narration: To sum up: the electron’s total energy in the nth level is minus thirteen point six over n squared electronvolts, negative because it is bound. Each jump downwards gives a photon carrying the energy difference, with a wavelength given by the Rydberg formula. Lines ending on levels one to five form the Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Write n₁ for the lower level and n₂ for the upper: 1/λ is always positive.
Give wavelengths in nm (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m) and name the series and region when asked.
For the series limit put n₂ = ∞; for the first line put n₂ = n₁ + 1.
Explain negative energy as "bound": zero is the free electron at rest at infinity.

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: Always take the lower level as n one and the upper as n two, so the reciprocal of the wavelength comes out positive. Give wavelengths in nanometres and name the series and the region. For a series limit, the upper level is infinity. And when asked why the energy is negative, say that the electron is bound, with zero meaning a free electron at rest far away.

sections.heading: 1. The alpha-scattering experiment and Rutherford’s model
sections.body_md:
- **Thomson’s model:** positive charge spread uniformly through the atom, electrons embedded in it; it predicts only tiny deflections of α particles and none thrown back.
- **Geiger–Marsden experiment (1909–1913):** a narrow beam of α particles from a radioactive source in a lead block falls on a very thin gold foil in an evacuated chamber; a zinc sulphide screen with a microscope, turned round the foil, counts the scintillations at each scattering angle θ.
- **Observations → conclusions:** (i) most α particles pass straight through or are deflected by a degree or two → the atom is mostly empty space; (ii) a few are deflected through large angles → the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny region; (iii) about 1 in several thousand is turned back (θ > 90°) → that region also holds nearly all the mass.
- **Rutherford’s nuclear model:** a tiny, massive, positively charged **nucleus** (radius about $10^{-15}$–$10^{-14}$ m) with electrons revolving round it at distances of about $10^{-10}$ m; the electrons are too light (about 1/7300 of an α particle’s mass) to deflect α particles appreciably.
- The mathematical theory of α scattering (the impact-parameter formula and Rutherford’s scattering formula) is **not** in the ISC syllabus.

key_terms.definition_md: A tiny flash of light produced when an α particle strikes a zinc sulphide screen.
The tiny central part of an atom that contains all its positive charge and nearly all its mass.

sections.heading: 2. Distance of closest approach; limits of Rutherford’s model
sections.body_md:
- An α particle (charge 2e) of kinetic energy K aimed **head-on** at a nucleus (charge Ze) stops momentarily at the **distance of closest approach** d, where all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy (nucleus treated as fixed):
$$K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2Ze^2}{d}\quad\Rightarrow\quad d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2Ze^2}{K}$$
- d is an **upper limit** to the radius of the nucleus; d ∝ Z/K. Use 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J; $\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 1.44$ MeV fm.
- Example: 5.0 MeV α on gold (Z = 79): d = 4.55 × 10⁻¹⁴ m ≈ 45.5 fm; the atom (≈ 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) is about 3000 times larger.
- **Limitations of Rutherford’s model:** an orbiting electron is accelerated and should radiate (classical electromagnetism), spiralling into the nucleus in about $10^{-8}$ s, so atoms would be unstable; the radiated frequency would change continuously, giving a continuous spectrum instead of the observed line spectrum.

sections.heading: 3. Bohr’s postulates; radius and speed of the nth orbit
sections.body_md:
- **Postulates (hydrogen):** (1) the electron revolves in certain circular **stationary orbits** without radiating, the Coulomb force providing the centripetal force; (2) in these orbits the angular momentum is quantised: $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, n = 1, 2, 3, … (n the principal quantum number); (3) a photon is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits: $h\nu = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}$.
- **Radius (derivation):** $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$ and $v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi m r}$ give $r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 n^2h^2}{\pi m e^2} = 0.53\,n^2$ Å; r ∝ n², radii 1 : 4 : 9 : 16; r₁ = 0.53 Å is the Bohr radius.
- **Speed (derivation):** dividing $mv^2r = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ by $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$: $v_n = \dfrac{e^2}{2\varepsilon_0 nh} = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^6}{n}$ m s⁻¹; v ∝ 1/n; v₁ ≈ c/137.
- Frequency of revolution $\dfrac{v}{2\pi r} \propto \dfrac{1}{n^3}$; linear momentum mv ∝ 1/n; angular momentum ∝ n.

key_terms.definition_md: An allowed Bohr orbit in which the electron does not radiate energy.

sections.heading: 4. Energy of the electron; meaning of negative energy
sections.body_md:
- **Kinetic energy:** $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$; **potential energy:** $U = -\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$; **total:** $E = K + U = -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$, so K = −E and U = 2E.
- With $r_n$: $E_n = -\dfrac{me^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2 n^2 h^2} = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$ eV; E₁ = −13.6, E₂ = −3.40, E₃ = −1.51, E₄ = −0.85 eV, E∞ = 0.
- **Negative total energy** means the electron is **bound** to the nucleus: zero is the free electron at rest far away, so energy must be supplied to remove it. The more negative E, the more tightly bound.
- **Ionisation energy** from level n: 13.6/n² eV (13.6 eV from the ground state; ionisation potential 13.6 V). **Excitation energy:** E_n − E₁ (10.2 eV to n = 2, 12.09 eV to n = 3).
- As n increases, E and U increase (towards zero) while K and v decrease.

sections.heading: 5. Energy-level diagram and the five series
sections.body_md:
- The **energy-level diagram** shows the allowed energies as horizontal lines (n = 1 at −13.6 eV, crowding together towards 0 at n = ∞). A downward jump emits a photon $h\nu = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}$; an upward jump needs exactly that energy to be absorbed.
- **Series** (lines ending on the same lower level n₁): **Lyman** n₁ = 1, ultraviolet (91.2–121.5 nm); **Balmer** n₁ = 2, visible and near ultraviolet (364.6–656.3 nm; the lines from n₂ = 3–6 are visible); **Paschen** n₁ = 3, infrared (820–1875 nm); **Brackett** n₁ = 4, infrared (1459–4051 nm); **Pfund** n₁ = 5, far infrared (2279–7458 nm).
- The infrared series overlap; Lyman and Balmer do not.
- Atoms excited to level n can emit $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ different lines. Cool hydrogen (all in n = 1) absorbs only Lyman lines.

sections.heading: 6. The Rydberg formula; successes and limits of Bohr’s model
sections.body_md:
- From $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}$: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$ with $R = \dfrac{me^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2ch^3} = 1.097 \times 10^7$ m⁻¹ (the **Rydberg constant**). Equivalently λ (nm) = 1240/ΔE (eV).
- **Method:** n₁ is the lower level (it fixes the series), n₂ the upper. Series limit $\lambda_\infty = n_1^2/R$; first line n₂ = n₁ + 1. To identify a line, decide the series from the wavelength range, then solve for n₂.
- Example: 5 → 2 gives 1/λ = 1.097 × 10⁷ × 0.21, λ = 434 nm (Balmer, violet). A line at 1282 nm is Paschen 5 → 3.
- A graph of 1/λ against 1/n₂² for one series is a straight line of slope −R.
- **Successes:** stability, size and ionisation energy of hydrogen, all its wavelengths. **Limits:** only one-electron atoms; no line intensities or fine structure; quantum rules assumed, not explained.

key_terms.definition_md: The constant R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ in the formula for the wave numbers of the hydrogen lines.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Pair each α-scattering observation with its conclusion; for closest approach use charge 2e and 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J.
- Bohr derivations: start from mv²/r = e²/(4πε₀r²) and mvr = nh/2π; end with r ∝ n², v ∝ 1/n, E ∝ −1/n².
- Negative energy = bound electron; ionisation energy from level n is 13.6/n² eV.
- Rydberg formula with n₁ the lower level; give λ in nm and name the series and region.

cards.front_md: Thomson’s model of the atom?
cards.back_md: Positive charge spread evenly through the atom, electrons embedded in it.

cards.front_md: What did Geiger and Marsden fire at a thin gold foil?
cards.back_md: A narrow beam of α particles; they counted scintillations on a ZnS screen at each angle.

cards.front_md: Why was the scattering chamber evacuated?
cards.back_md: So that air molecules would not stop or scatter the α particles.

cards.front_md: Most α particles pass straight through. Conclusion?
cards.back_md: The atom is mostly empty space.

cards.front_md: A very few α particles bounce back. Conclusion?
cards.back_md: Positive charge and nearly all the mass are packed into a tiny nucleus.

cards.front_md: Why do the electrons hardly deflect α particles?
cards.back_md: An electron has only about 1/7300 of the α particle’s mass.

cards.front_md: Distance of closest approach?
cards.back_md: $d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2Ze^2}{K}$, where all the α’s kinetic energy has become potential energy.

cards.front_md: How does d depend on K and Z?
cards.back_md: d ∝ Z/K: double the energy, half the distance.

cards.front_md: Typical sizes of an atom and a nucleus?
cards.back_md: Atom ~10⁻¹⁰ m; nucleus ~10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹⁴ m.

cards.front_md: Two failures of Rutherford’s model?
cards.back_md: An orbiting (accelerated) electron should radiate and spiral in: no stable atoms; and it would give a continuous, not a line, spectrum.

cards.front_md: Bohr’s quantum condition?
cards.back_md: $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, n = 1, 2, 3, …

cards.front_md: Bohr’s frequency condition?
cards.back_md: $h\nu = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}$: one photon per jump.

cards.front_md: Radius of the nth orbit of hydrogen?
cards.back_md: $r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 n^2h^2}{\pi me^2} = 0.53\,n^2$ Å.

cards.front_md: Speed in the nth orbit of hydrogen?
cards.back_md: $v_n = \dfrac{e^2}{2\varepsilon_0 nh} = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^6}{n}$ m s⁻¹.

cards.front_md: How do r, v and the revolution frequency scale with n?
cards.back_md: r ∝ n², v ∝ 1/n, frequency ∝ 1/n³.

cards.front_md: K, U and E of the electron in terms of r?
cards.back_md: K = e²/(8πε₀r), U = −e²/(4πε₀r), E = −e²/(8πε₀r).

cards.front_md: Relations between K, U and E in a Bohr orbit?
cards.back_md: K = −E and U = 2E.

cards.front_md: Energy of the nth level of hydrogen?
What does the negative total energy mean?
cards.back_md: The electron is bound: energy must be supplied to free it (E = 0 is the free electron at rest far away).

cards.front_md: Ionisation energy of hydrogen from level n?
cards.back_md: 13.6/n² eV (13.6 eV from the ground state).

cards.front_md: n = 4 level: K, U, E?
Rydberg formula?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$, R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, n₁ the lower level.

cards.front_md: Series ending on n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?
cards.back_md: Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund.

cards.front_md: Region of each hydrogen series?
cards.back_md: Lyman UV; Balmer visible and near UV; Paschen, Brackett IR; Pfund far IR.

cards.front_md: Series limit?
cards.back_md: Shortest wavelength of a series (n₂ = ∞): λ = n₁²/R.

cards.front_md: Line from n = 5 to n = 2?
cards.back_md: Balmer, 434 nm, violet.

cards.front_md: Number of lines from atoms excited to level n?
Why does cool hydrogen absorb only Lyman lines?
cards.back_md: Almost all its atoms are in n = 1, so every absorption starts there.

cards.front_md: Two limitations of Bohr’s model?
cards.back_md: Fails for many-electron atoms; cannot explain line intensities or fine structure.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: identifying an infrared line?
cards.back_md: The IR series overlap: test the possible n₁ values with the Rydberg formula and look for a whole-number n₂.

questions.stem_md: Which result of the Geiger–Marsden experiment could not be explained if the positive charge of each gold atom were spread evenly through its whole volume, as in Thomson’s model?

options.text_md: Some α particles were turned back through more than 90°
Most α particles passed through the foil almost undeflected
The gold atoms in the foil were electrically neutral
Some α particles were deflected by a fraction of a degree

questions.solution_md: In Thomson’s model the forces on an α particle inside an atom are weak and spread out, so only small deflections are possible. It accounts for nearly undeflected particles and for neutral atoms, but no spread-out charge can reverse a fast, heavy α particle — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the Geiger–Marsden apparatus, the α source, the gold foil and the zinc sulphide screen were all inside a chamber from which the air had been pumped out. This was done mainly

options.text_md: to stop the thin gold foil from melting
so that the zinc sulphide screen would glow more brightly
so that air molecules would not slow down, stop or scatter the α particles
to remove the electrons from the gold atoms

questions.solution_md: α particles lose energy quickly in air (their range is only a few centimetres) and are scattered by air molecules; in a vacuum any deflection is due to the foil alone — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The gold foil (Z = 79) in an α-scattering experiment is replaced by an aluminium foil (Z = 13) with the same number of atoms per unit area. The number of α particles scattered through large angles

options.text_md: decreases, because the repulsion from each nucleus is much weaker
increases, because aluminium nuclei are lighter
stays the same, because the number of nuclei in the path is the same
decreases, because aluminium atoms have fewer electrons to deflect the α particles

questions.solution_md: A large deflection needs a close encounter with a strong repulsion. The Coulomb force on the α particle is proportional to Z, so with Z = 13 an α particle must pass much nearer a nucleus to be turned through a large angle, and fewer do so. The electrons play almost no part — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A proton and an α particle move with the same speed, and each is aimed head-on at the same gold nucleus. Taking the mass of the α particle as four times that of the proton, the ratio of the distance of closest approach of the proton to that of the α particle is
questions.solution_md: $d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{qZe}{K}$ with $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. The proton has half the charge and, at the same speed, a quarter of the kinetic energy, so $\dfrac{d_p}{d_\alpha} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 = 2$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An α particle aimed head-on at a nucleus has a distance of closest approach d. When it is still at a distance 4d from the centre of the nucleus, the fraction of its initial kinetic energy that it still has is
questions.solution_md: At d the potential energy equals the initial kinetic energy $K_0$. Since $U \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$, at 4d it is $\dfrac{K_0}{4}$, so the kinetic energy left is $K_0 - \dfrac{K_0}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}K_0$ — option (b). 1/4 is the part already converted; 15/16 would follow from a $1/r^2$ energy.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In explaining the α-scattering results, Rutherford could ignore the electrons of the gold atoms, because an electron is far too light to turn a fast α particle through an appreciable angle.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. An electron has only about 1/7300 of the mass of an α particle; in an encounter the electron is pushed aside and the α particle’s path barely changes. The large deflections must come from the heavy nucleus.

questions.stem_md: An α particle aimed straight at a gold nucleus stops for an instant and then turns back. The least distance between the α particle and the centre of the nucleus during this motion is called the distance of ___.
questions.solution_md: The **distance of closest approach**: there the α particle’s kinetic energy has all become electrostatic potential energy.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An α particle fired head-on at a heavy nucleus comes to rest for an instant before moving back the way it came.

**Reason (R):** At its closest point to the nucleus, the whole of the α particle’s initial kinetic energy has been stored as electrostatic potential energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: with all the kinetic energy converted, the speed at that point is zero, so the α particle is momentarily at rest before the repulsion drives it back — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The electrons in a gold foil cause hardly any deflection of the α particles passing through it.

**Reason (R):** Electrons carry negative charge, while α particles carry positive charge.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A: the electrons do attract the α particles, yet they barely deflect them because an electron has only about 1/7300 of the α particle’s mass — option (b).

questions.stem_md: An α particle of kinetic energy 5.5 MeV is aimed head-on at a silver nucleus (Z = 47). Find its distance of closest approach, in femtometres (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m), to 3 significant figures. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

What minimum kinetic energy, in MeV, must an α particle have to get within 15 fm (1.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m) of the centre of a tin nucleus (Z = 50) in a head-on approach? (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: $K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2Ze^2}{d} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 50 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{1.5 \times 10^{-14}} = 1.536 \times 10^{-12}$ J $= \dfrac{1.536 \times 10^{-12}}{1.6 \times 10^{-13}} = 9.6$ MeV.

questions.stem_md: An α particle of mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg moving at 1.6 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ is aimed head-on at a gold nucleus (Z = 79). Find its distance of closest approach, in fm, to 3 significant figures. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

Imagine a hydrogen atom enlarged until its nucleus, of radius about 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, is as big as a cricket ball of radius 3.6 cm. Taking the radius of the atom as 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, what would the radius of the enlarged atom be, in km (2 significant figures)?
questions.solution_md: Scale factor $\dfrac{0.53 \times 10^{-10}}{1.0 \times 10^{-15}} = 5.3 \times 10^{4}$, so the atom’s radius becomes $3.6 \times 5.3 \times 10^{4}$ cm $= 1.9 \times 10^{5}$ cm $= 1.9$ km: a ball in the middle of a town-sized empty sphere.

questions.stem_md: An α particle of kinetic energy 7.2 MeV approaches a uranium nucleus (Z = 92) head-on. At what distance from the centre of the nucleus has its kinetic energy fallen to half its initial value? Answer in fm (3 significant figures). (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: Half the kinetic energy, 3.6 MeV, has become potential energy: $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2Ze^2}{r} = 3.6$ MeV $= 5.76 \times 10^{-13}$ J, so $r = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 92 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{5.76 \times 10^{-13}} = 7.36 \times 10^{-14}$ m $= 73.6$ fm, twice the distance of closest approach (36.8 fm).

marking_scheme.step: U = K₀/2 = 3.6 MeV at the required point

questions.stem_md: A student fires α particles of 3.5 MeV head-on at gold nuclei (Z = 79), calculates a distance of closest approach of about 65 fm, and concludes that “the radius of a gold nucleus is 65 fm”. Evaluate this conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md: The calculation is right ($d = 65.0$ fm), but the conclusion is not. The α particle stops at 65 fm only because the Coulomb repulsion has used up its kinetic energy; it never touches the nucleus. So 65 fm is only an **upper limit** to the radius. Faster α particles get closer ($d \propto 1/K$), and such experiments show that a gold nucleus is really only about 7 fm in radius.

questions.solution_md: d = k(2e)(Ze)/K is an upper limit, not the radius.

marking_scheme.step: d is only an upper limit: the α particle never reaches the nucleus
Higher K gives smaller d; the true radius is smaller (about 7 fm)

questions.stem_md: In a Geiger–Marsden type experiment, the detector counts α particles for equal times at 5°, then at 60° and finally at 170° from the direction of the beam. Describe how the three counts compare, and state what each result tells us about the structure of the atom.

answer.model_answer_md: At **5°** the count is very large: most α particles pass through the foil with little or no deflection, so most of the atom is **empty space**. At **60°** the count is far smaller: only the few α particles that pass very close to a nucleus feel a strong enough repulsion, so the **positive charge is concentrated in a tiny region**. At **170°** only an occasional α particle is counted: turning a fast α particle right back needs a nearly head-on encounter with something **massive** as well as highly charged, so nearly all the mass of the atom is in that tiny **nucleus**.

questions.solution_md: Counts fall steeply with angle: empty space, concentrated charge, massive nucleus.

marking_scheme.step: 5°: very many → atom mostly empty space
60°: few → positive charge concentrated in a tiny region
170°: very few but not zero → small, massive nucleus

questions.stem_md: Use classical electromagnetic theory to explain why an atom built according to Rutherford’s model should (a) be unstable, (b) give out a continuous spectrum.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) An electron moving in a circular orbit is accelerated towards the nucleus, and an accelerated charge radiates electromagnetic energy. Losing energy, the electron would spiral into the nucleus (in about 10⁻⁸ s), so the atom would collapse. (b) As the orbit shrank, the frequency of revolution, and so of the emitted radiation, would rise continuously, so the atom would emit a continuous range of frequencies instead of the sharp lines observed.

questions.solution_md: Accelerated charge radiates; changing frequency gives a continuous spectrum.

marking_scheme.step: Accelerated electron radiates and spirals in: atom unstable

questions.stem_md: Obtain an expression for the distance of closest approach d of an α particle of kinetic energy K aimed head-on at a nucleus of atomic number Z. Hence find d for α particles of 4.8 MeV aimed at lead nuclei (Z = 82). (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

answer.model_answer_md:
The α particle (charge 2e) slows down as it approaches; the much heavier nucleus is taken as fixed. At the closest point its speed is zero, so all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy:
$K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{(2e)(Ze)}{d}$, so $d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2Ze^2}{K}$.
Here $K = 4.8 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13} = 7.68 \times 10^{-13}$ J: $d = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 82 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{7.68 \times 10^{-13}} = 4.92 \times 10^{-14}$ m, about 49 fm.

questions.solution_md: Energy conservation: K = k(2e)(Ze)/d.

marking_scheme.step: At closest approach K is all electrostatic PE (speed zero)

questions.stem_md: Match each result of the α-scattering experiment in Column A with what it shows about the atom in Column B.

options.text_md: Nearly all the α particles reach a detector placed directly behind the foil
A small number are scattered through large angles
An occasional α particle rebounds towards the source
Foils of higher atomic number scatter more α particles through large angles

match_right.text_md: Nearly all the mass is in that small region
The atom is mostly empty space
The repulsion grows with the nuclear charge Ze
The positive charge occupies a very small region

questions.solution_md: Undeflected → empty space (1 → q); large angles → charge concentrated (2 → s); rebound → massive nucleus (3 → p); more scattering at higher Z → repulsion ∝ Ze (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe, with a labelled diagram (described in words), the Geiger–Marsden α-scattering experiment. [2] (b) State Rutherford’s two main conclusions from it. [1] (c) Find the distance of closest approach of a 7.0 MeV α particle aimed head-on at a platinum nucleus (Z = 78), and explain why this is only an upper limit to the size of the nucleus. [2] (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A radioactive source in a lead block sends α particles through narrow slits as a fine beam onto a very thin gold foil. A zinc sulphide screen, viewed through a microscope, can be turned round the foil on a circular scale; each α particle striking it gives a flash (scintillation), and the flashes are counted at each scattering angle θ. The whole apparatus is in an evacuated chamber so that air does not stop or scatter the α particles.

(b) The atom is mostly empty space; its positive charge and nearly all its mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus (about $10^{-14}$ m across), with the electrons outside it.

(c) $K = 7.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13} = 1.12 \times 10^{-12}$ J; $d = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 78 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{1.12 \times 10^{-12}} = 3.21 \times 10^{-14}$ m ≈ 32.1 fm. The α particle turns back before touching the nucleus, so the nucleus can only be smaller than d.

questions.solution_md: Apparatus, conclusions, then d = k(2e)(Ze)/K.

marking_scheme.step: Source, slits, thin gold foil, ZnS screen and microscope
Rotating detector, vacuum, counts at each angle
Mostly empty; tiny, massive, positive nucleus
Upper limit: the α particle never reaches the nucleus

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT one of Bohr’s postulates for the hydrogen atom?

options.text_md: The angular momentum of the electron in an allowed orbit is a whole-number multiple of h/2π
A photon is emitted only when the electron jumps from a higher allowed orbit to a lower one
The Coulomb attraction of the nucleus provides the centripetal force on the electron
The electron radiates energy continuously as it revolves in an allowed orbit

questions.solution_md: Bohr postulated that the electron does **not** radiate while it stays in an allowed (stationary) orbit; radiation is emitted only in a jump, as one photon of energy E₂ − E₁ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The radius of a certain Bohr orbit of hydrogen is 16 times the radius of the first orbit. The angular momentum of the electron in this orbit is ___ times h/2π.
questions.solution_md: r ∝ n², so n² = 16 and n = 4; then mvr = nh/2π = **4** h/2π.

questions.stem_md: Taking the radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen as 0.53 Å, find the radius of the n = 7 orbit, in nm (3 significant figures).
In one of the Bohr orbits of hydrogen, the electron moves at 5.5 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Taking its speed in the first orbit as 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, find the quantum number n of this orbit.
As the electron of a hydrogen atom is moved to orbits of larger n, which one of these quantities increases?

options.text_md: its kinetic energy
its orbital speed
its frequency of revolution
its total energy

questions.solution_md: E = −13.6/n² eV rises towards zero (becomes less negative), while K = 13.6/n² eV, v ∝ 1/n and the frequency of revolution ∝ 1/n³ all fall — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The ratio of the linear momentum of the electron in the n = 2 orbit of hydrogen to its linear momentum in the n = 6 orbit is
questions.solution_md: p = mv and v ∝ 1/n, so p₂ : p₆ = 6 : 2 = 3 : 1 — option (d). (Angular momentum mvr ∝ n goes the other way, 1 : 3.)

questions.stem_md: Find the kinetic energy of the electron in the n = 7 level of hydrogen, in eV (3 significant figures). (Ground-state energy −13.6 eV)
Find the potential energy of the electron in the first excited state of hydrogen, in eV. (Ground-state energy −13.6 eV)
questions.solution_md: First excited state: n = 2, $E_2 = -\dfrac{13.6}{4} = -3.4$ eV, and $U = 2E = -6.8$ eV.

questions.stem_md: A hydrogen atom has its electron in the n = 5 level. How much energy, in eV, is needed to ionise it? (Ground-state energy −13.6 eV; 3 significant figures)
questions.solution_md: Ionisation takes the electron from $E_5 = -\dfrac{13.6}{25} = -0.544$ eV up to 0: $0 - (-0.544) = 0.544$ eV.

questions.stem_md: How much energy, in eV, must a hydrogen atom absorb to move its electron from the n = 4 level to the n = 6 level? (Ground-state energy −13.6 eV; 3 significant figures)
A hydrogen atom in its ground state absorbs a photon of energy 13.06 eV. Its electron is raised to the level

options.text_md: n = ∞, so the atom is ionised

questions.solution_md: After absorption $E = -13.6 + 13.06 = -0.54$ eV $= -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$, so $n^2 = 25$ and $n = 5$ — option (c). 13.06 eV is less than 13.6 eV, so the atom is not ionised.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The radius of the second Bohr orbit of hydrogen is twice the radius of the first.

**Reason (R):** The radius of the nth Bohr orbit is proportional to n².

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: r₂ = 4r₁ = 2.12 Å. R is true, and it is exactly what shows A to be wrong — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The total energy of the electron in the ground state of hydrogen is −13.6 eV. Explain the significance of the negative sign, and state what happens to the electron if the atom absorbs 15.0 eV.

answer.model_answer_md: Zero energy is taken as the electron at rest infinitely far from the proton. A negative total energy means the electron has less energy than this: it is **bound** to the nucleus, and 13.6 eV must be supplied to free it. With 15.0 eV the electron is freed (the atom is ionised), and it moves away with the remaining 15.0 − 13.6 = 1.4 eV as kinetic energy.

questions.solution_md: Negative energy = bound state; excess over 13.6 eV becomes kinetic energy.

marking_scheme.step: Negative E: electron bound; zero is the free electron at rest at infinity
Atom ionised; electron leaves with 1.4 eV

questions.stem_md: Starting from Bohr’s quantum condition and the fact that the Coulomb attraction provides the centripetal force, show that the radius of the nth orbit of the hydrogen atom is r_n = ε₀n²h²/(πme²). Evaluate r₁, taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

answer.model_answer_md:
Centripetal force from the Coulomb attraction: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$, i.e. $mv^2r = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ (1). Quantum condition: $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, so $v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr}$ (2).
Put (2) in (1): $m\cdot\dfrac{n^2h^2}{4\pi^2m^2r^2}\cdot r = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$, so $r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 n^2h^2}{\pi me^2}$.
For n = 1: $r_1 = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times (6.6 \times 10^{-34})^2}{\pi \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2} = 5.27 \times 10^{-11}$ m ≈ 0.53 Å.

questions.solution_md: Combine mv²r = e²/4πε₀ with mvr = nh/2π.

questions.stem_md: Using Bohr’s postulates, show that the speed of the electron in the nth orbit of hydrogen is v_n = e²/(2ε₀nh), and calculate it for n = 3. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

answer.model_answer_md:
From $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}$: $mv^2r = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$. Dividing by $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$: $v = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}{nh} = \dfrac{e^2}{2\varepsilon_0nh}$.
For n = 3: $v_3 = \dfrac{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 3 \times 6.6 \times 10^{-34}} = 7.30 \times 10^{5}$ m s⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Divide mv²r = e²/4πε₀ by mvr = nh/2π.

marking_scheme.step: v_n = e²/(2ε₀nh) from the two conditions

questions.stem_md: Derive expressions for the kinetic energy, the potential energy and the total energy of the electron in the nth orbit of the hydrogen atom in terms of the orbit radius r_n. Hence show that the kinetic energy is equal in magnitude to the total energy and the potential energy is twice the total energy.

answer.model_answer_md:
From $\dfrac{mv^2}{r_n} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_n^2}$: $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r_n}$.
The potential energy of charge −e at distance $r_n$ from +e: $U = -\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_n}$.
Total: $E = K + U = -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r_n}$. So $K = -E = |E|$ and $U = 2E$ (both negative).

questions.solution_md: K from the force equation; U = −e²/(4πε₀r); E = K + U.

questions.stem_md: When the electron of a hydrogen atom falls from the n = 6 level to the n = 3 level, find the changes in its kinetic energy and its potential energy. Explain how the atom loses energy even though the electron’s kinetic energy increases.

answer.model_answer_md: $K = \dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$ eV: $0.378 \to 1.511$, so ΔK = +1.13 eV. $U = -\dfrac{27.2}{n^2}$ eV: $-0.756 \to -3.022$, so $Delta U = -2.27$ eV. The potential energy falls by **twice** as much as the kinetic energy rises, so the total energy falls by 1.13 eV, which leaves the atom as a photon.

questions.solution_md: ΔU = −2ΔK, so ΔE = −ΔK.

marking_scheme.step: U falls twice as much as K rises: ΔE = −1.13 eV, emitted as a photon

questions.stem_md: A muon has the same charge as an electron but about 207 times its mass. In “muonic hydrogen” a muon orbits a proton. Treating the proton as fixed, Bohr’s theory gives the radius of the first orbit as about

options.text_md: 0.53 Å, the same as for hydrogen

questions.solution_md: $r_1 = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0h^2}{\pi me^2} \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$, so the orbit shrinks by the factor 207: $\dfrac{0.53 \times 10^{-10}}{207} = 2.6 \times 10^{-13}$ m — option (c).

questions.stem_md: When the electron of a hydrogen atom jumps from the n = 3 level to the n = 1 level, its kinetic energy and its potential energy change by

options.text_md: −12.09 eV and +24.18 eV respectively
+12.09 eV and −24.18 eV respectively
+12.09 eV and −12.09 eV respectively
−12.09 eV and −12.09 eV respectively

questions.solution_md: $K = \dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$: $1.51 \to 13.6$ eV, ΔK = +12.09 eV. $U = -\dfrac{27.2}{n^2}$: $-3.02 \to -27.2$ eV, $Delta U = -24.18$ eV. The total falls by 12.09 eV, carried off by the photon — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? An electron near a proton whose total energy is +2.0 eV is bound to the proton in one of the Bohr orbits.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Bound states of hydrogen have negative total energy (−13.6/n² eV). With a positive total energy the electron is free: it can escape to a large distance, still having 2.0 eV of kinetic energy there.

questions.stem_md: The electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen moves at 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. How many times greater is the speed of light, 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹? Give the answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{2.2 \times 10^{6}} = 136$: the electron moves at about 1/137 of the speed of light, so non-relativistic mechanics is a fair approximation.

questions.stem_md: The total energy of the electron in a hydrogen atom is −0.378 eV. Find (a) the quantum number n of its orbit, (b) the radius of the orbit and the speed of the electron, (c) its kinetic and potential energies. (E₁ = −13.6 eV, r₁ = 0.53 Å, v₁ = 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: n from E; r ∝ n², v ∝ 1/n; K = −E, U = 2E.

questions.stem_md: (a) State Bohr’s postulates for the hydrogen atom. [1] (b) Using them, derive an expression for the radius of the nth orbit. [2] (c) The electron of a hydrogen atom moves in an orbit of radius 33.92 Å. Find the quantum number of the orbit, and the speed and kinetic energy of the electron in it. [2] (r₁ = 0.53 Å, v₁ = 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, E₁ = −13.6 eV)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The electron revolves in certain circular orbits without radiating; in them its angular momentum is $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$; it emits or absorbs a photon $h\nu = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}$ only when it jumps between orbits.

(b) $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}$ gives $mv^2r = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$; with $v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr}$: $\dfrac{n^2h^2}{4\pi^2mr} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$, so $r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0n^2h^2}{\pi me^2}$.

(c) $n^2 = \dfrac{33.92}{0.53} = 64$, so n = 8. $v_8 = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^{6}}{8} = 2.75 \times 10^{5}$ m s⁻¹; $K = \dfrac{13.6}{64} \approx 0.21$ eV.

questions.solution_md: Postulates; force + quantum condition; r ∝ n², v ∝ 1/n, K = 13.6/n².

questions.stem_md: (a) Obtain the total energy of the electron in the nth orbit of hydrogen in terms of the orbit radius r_n, and hence show that E_n = −13.6/n² eV (you may quote r_n = ε₀n²h²/(πme²) and use me⁴/(8ε₀²h²) = 13.6 eV). [2] (b) Explain the significance of the negative sign of E_n. [1] (c) A hydrogen atom is in its first excited state. Find the minimum energy needed to ionise it and the longest wavelength of light that can do so. [2] (hc = 1240 eV nm)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r_n}$ (from the force equation) and $U = -\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_n}$, so $E_n = -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r_n}$. With $r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0n^2h^2}{\pi me^2}$: $E_n = -\dfrac{me^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2n^2h^2} = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$ eV.

(b) Zero is the free electron at rest far away; negative energy means the electron is bound, and energy $13.6/n^2$ eV must be supplied to free it.

(c) First excited state: n = 2, $E_2 = -3.4$ eV, so the ionisation energy is 3.4 eV. Longest wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E} = \dfrac{1240}{3.4} = 365$ nm (near ultraviolet; it equals the Balmer series limit).

questions.solution_md: E = K + U; bound state; λ_max = hc/E_ion.

questions.stem_md: State two limitations of Bohr’s model of the atom, and explain the reason for one of them.

answer.model_answer_md: Any two: (i) it applies only to hydrogen and one-electron ions such as He⁺ and Li²⁺, not to many-electron atoms; (ii) it cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines; (iii) it cannot explain the fine structure (close splitting) of lines; (iv) its postulates are assumed, not derived. Reason for (i): in a many-electron atom each electron is also repelled by the other electrons, and Bohr’s model, which considers only the attraction of the nucleus, has no way of including this.

questions.solution_md: One-electron systems only; intensities; fine structure.

marking_scheme.step: Correct reason for one (e.g. electron–electron repulsion ignored)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Bohr’s theory cannot give the correct energy levels of a neutral helium atom.

**Reason (R):** Bohr’s theory does not take into account the repulsion between the electrons of a many-electron atom.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: neutral helium has two electrons, each repelled by the other as well as attracted by the nucleus; Bohr’s single-electron treatment leaves this out, so its levels are wrong — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Compare Rutherford’s and Bohr’s models of the hydrogen atom with respect to (a) the stability of the atom, (b) the spectrum it should emit, (c) the possible sizes of the electron’s orbit. Which model agrees better with experiment, and why?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Rutherford: the orbiting electron should radiate and spiral into the nucleus, so the atom is unstable. Bohr: in stationary orbits the electron does not radiate, so the atom is stable in its ground state. (b) Rutherford: a continuous spectrum as the orbit shrinks. Bohr: photons only in jumps between fixed levels, hν = E₂ − E₁, so a line spectrum. (c) Rutherford: any radius. Bohr: only r = 0.53 n² Å. **Bohr’s model agrees better** for hydrogen: it predicts stable atoms of the right size (0.53 Å), the ionisation energy of 13.6 eV and every observed wavelength. It keeps Rutherford’s nucleus, so it builds on, rather than replaces, his model.

questions.solution_md: Stability, spectrum, orbit sizes: Bohr matches observation.

marking_scheme.step: Spectrum: continuous vs lines; orbits: any vs r ∝ n²
Bohr better: right size, 13.6 eV, wavelengths

questions.stem_md: The spectral line emitted when the electron of a hydrogen atom drops from the n = 6 level to the n = 3 level belongs to the

options.text_md: Balmer series, in the visible region
Paschen series, in the infrared
Brackett series, in the infrared
Lyman series, in the ultraviolet

questions.solution_md: The series is fixed by the lower level: $n_1 = 3$ is the Paschen series. $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{R(1/9 - 1/36)} = 1094$ nm, in the infrared — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which one of these electron jumps in a hydrogen atom gives out visible light?
questions.solution_md: Wavelengths from $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$: 3 → 2: 656.3 nm (red, visible) — option (b); 3 → 1: 102.6 nm (UV); 5 → 3: 1282 nm (IR); 7 → 5: 4.65 μm (far IR).

questions.stem_md: In the formula 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) for the wavelengths of hydrogen, the Rydberg constant R = 1.097 × 10⁷ is expressed in the SI unit ___.
questions.solution_md: The bracket is a pure number, so R has the unit of 1/λ: **m⁻¹** (per metre).

questions.stem_md: Find the wavelength of the first (longest-wavelength) line of the Brackett series of hydrogen, in μm (3 significant figures). (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: Brackett: $n_1 = 4$; first line $n_2 = 5$. $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{16} - \dfrac{1}{25}\right) = 1.097 \times 10^{7} \times \dfrac{9}{400} = 2.468 \times 10^{5}$ m⁻¹, so $\lambda = 4.05 \times 10^{-6}$ m $= 4.05$ μm (infrared).

questions.stem_md: Find the series limit (shortest wavelength) of the Brackett series of hydrogen, in nm (4 significant figures). (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)
Calculate the wavelength of the hydrogen line produced when the electron falls from the n = 6 level to the n = 2 level, in nm (3 significant figures). (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{36}\right) = R \times \dfrac{2}{9} = 2.438 \times 10^{6}$ m⁻¹, so $\lambda = 410.2$ nm ≈ 410 nm: a Balmer line, violet, at the edge of the visible.

questions.stem_md: Find the wavelength of the photon emitted when the electron of a hydrogen atom drops from the n = 3 level to the ground state, in nm (4 significant figures). (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = \dfrac{8R}{9} = 9.751 \times 10^{6}$ m⁻¹, so $\lambda = \dfrac{9}{8R} = 102.6$ nm (Lyman series, ultraviolet).

questions.stem_md: Find the ratio of the shortest wavelength of the Lyman series of hydrogen to the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series.
questions.solution_md: Series limits ($n_2 = \infty$): $\lambda_L = \dfrac{1}{R}$ and $\lambda_B = \dfrac{4}{R}$, so the ratio is $\dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$.

questions.stem_md: A sample of hydrogen gas is excited so that some of its atoms reach the n = 6 level. How many different spectral lines can the sample emit as these atoms return to the ground state?
questions.solution_md: Every pair of levels from 1 to 6 gives a different line: $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The series limit of the Balmer series of hydrogen, at about 365 nm, lies in the visible region of the spectrum.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. λ = 4/R = 364.6 nm is shorter than about 400 nm, so it lies in the (near) ultraviolet; only the Balmer lines from n = 3 to 6 are visible.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Some lines of the Brackett series of hydrogen have shorter wavelengths than the first line of the Paschen series.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The first Paschen line (4 → 3) is at 1875 nm, while the Brackett series runs from 4051 nm down to its limit at 1459 nm; its lines from n₂ = 9 upwards (e.g. 1818 nm) are shorter than 1875 nm. The infrared series overlap.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hydrogen at room temperature, placed in a beam of ultraviolet and visible light, absorbs only wavelengths that belong to the Lyman series.

**Reason (R):** At room temperature most hydrogen atoms are in the n = 2 level.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: almost all the atoms are in the ground state, so every absorption starts from n = 1, giving Lyman wavelengths. R is false: the thermal energy at room temperature (about 0.03 eV) is far too small to supply the 10.2 eV needed to reach n = 2 — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Every line of the Lyman series of hydrogen has a shorter wavelength than every line of the Balmer series.

**Reason (R):** Each Lyman photon carries at least 10.2 eV, while no Balmer photon carries more than 3.4 eV.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: λ = hc/E, and every Lyman energy (10.2–13.6 eV) exceeds every Balmer energy (1.89–3.4 eV), so the longest Lyman wavelength (121.5 nm) is shorter than the Balmer limit (364.6 nm) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each electron jump in a hydrogen atom in Column A with the wavelength of the photon it emits in Column B.
questions.solution_md: From 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²): 2 → 1 gives 121.5 nm (1 → r); 3 → 2 gives 656.3 nm (2 → p); 4 → 3 gives 1875 nm (3 → s); 6 → 4 gives 2625 nm (4 → q). Larger energy gaps give shorter wavelengths.

questions.stem_md: An infrared spectrometer records a hydrogen line at 1005 nm. Show that it cannot belong to the Lyman, Balmer or Brackett series, and identify the transition that produces it. (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)

answer.model_answer_md:
Ranges (series limit to first line): Lyman 91.2–121.5 nm; Balmer 364.6–656.3 nm; Brackett 1459–4051 nm. 1005 nm is longer than every Lyman and Balmer line and shorter than the Brackett limit, so it can only be a Paschen line ($n_1 = 3$, 820–1875 nm).
$\dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} = \dfrac{1}{R\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{1.097 \times 10^{7} \times 1005 \times 10^{-9}} = 0.0907$, so $\dfrac{1}{n_2^2} = 0.0204$ and $n_2 = 7.00 \approx 7$.
The line comes from the jump **7 → 3** (Paschen, infrared).

questions.solution_md: Rule out by range; solve the Rydberg formula with n₁ = 3.

questions.stem_md: Two lines of the Balmer series of hydrogen are measured at 656.3 nm (from n = 3) and 486.1 nm (from n = 4). Using only the difference of their wave numbers 1/λ, find the Rydberg constant, and use it to predict the series limit of the Balmer series.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{1}{\lambda_4} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_3} = R\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{16}\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right)\right] = R\left(\dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{16}\right) = \dfrac{7R}{144}$.
$\dfrac{1}{486.1 \times 10^{-9}} - \dfrac{1}{656.3 \times 10^{-9}} = 2.0572 \times 10^{6} - 1.5237 \times 10^{6} = 5.335 \times 10^{5}$ m⁻¹, so $R = \dfrac{144}{7} \times 5.335 \times 10^{5} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}$ m⁻¹.
Series limit: $\lambda_\infty = \dfrac{4}{R} = 3.645 \times 10^{-7}$ m $\approx 364.5$ nm.

questions.solution_md: The difference of wave numbers is R(1/9 − 1/16).

questions.stem_md: Using Bohr’s energy levels E_n = −me⁴/(8ε₀²n²h²), derive the formula for the wavelength of the line emitted when the electron of a hydrogen atom jumps from level n₂ to a lower level n₁, and write the Rydberg constant in terms of the fundamental constants. Show that R ≈ 1.1 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, taking me⁴/(8ε₀²h²) = 13.6 eV, h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

answer.model_answer_md:
The photon carries the energy difference: $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1} = \dfrac{me^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2h^2}\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$.
So $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$ with $R = \dfrac{me^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2ch^3}$.
$R = \dfrac{13.6 \text{ eV}}{hc} = \dfrac{13.6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}} = 1.10 \times 10^{7}$ m⁻¹ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: hc/λ = E₂ − E₁; R = me⁴/(8ε₀²ch³) = 13.6 eV/hc.

questions.stem_md: Light containing every wavelength from 50 nm to 2000 nm passes through hydrogen gas at room temperature. Explain which hydrogen series appears as dark lines in the transmitted light, and why the Balmer lines are not among them.

answer.model_answer_md: At room temperature almost every hydrogen atom is in the ground state (the thermal energy, about 0.03 eV, is far less than the 10.2 eV needed to reach n = 2). Absorption therefore always starts from n = 1, so the dark lines are the **Lyman series** (91–122 nm, ultraviolet). Balmer absorption would have to start from n = 2, and practically no atoms are there.

questions.solution_md: All atoms in n = 1: only Lyman absorption.

marking_scheme.step: Atoms in the ground state; absorption from n = 1 gives Lyman dark lines
Balmer absorption needs atoms in n = 2: practically none

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 7 level. How many different lines can they emit in all, and how many of these belong to the Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series taken together? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: In all: $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{7 \times 6}{2} = 21$ lines. Paschen lines end on n = 3 and start from n = 4–7 (4 lines); Brackett end on n = 4 from 5–7 (3); Pfund end on n = 5 from 6–7 (2): 9 lines together. (Of the rest, 6 are Lyman, 5 Balmer and 1, the jump 7 → 6, belongs to a further infrared series.)

questions.solution_md: Count pairs of levels; group by the lower level.

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw (describe in words) an energy-level diagram of hydrogen showing the levels n = 1 to 5 with their energies, and mark the transitions that give the first line of the Lyman, Balmer and Paschen series. [2] (b) State the region of the spectrum in which the Brackett and Pfund series lie. [1] (c) Calculate the longest and the shortest wavelengths of the Pfund series. [2] (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Horizontal lines at $E_n = -13.6/n^2$ eV: n = 1 at −13.6 eV, n = 2 at −3.40 eV, n = 3 at −1.51 eV, n = 4 at −0.85 eV, n = 5 at −0.54 eV, with E = 0 (n = ∞) at the top; the gaps shrink upwards. Downward arrows: 2 → 1 (first Lyman line), 3 → 2 (first Balmer line), 4 → 3 (first Paschen line).

(b) Both lie in the infrared (Pfund in the far infrared).

(c) Pfund: $n_1 = 5$. Longest, $n_2 = 6$: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{1}{36}\right) = \dfrac{11R}{900}$, $\lambda = 7.46 \times 10^{-6}$ m $= 7.46$ μm. Shortest (series limit, $n_2 = \infty$): $\lambda = \dfrac{25}{R} = 2.28 \times 10^{-6}$ m $= 2.28$ μm.

questions.solution_md: Levels −13.6/n²; first lines n₂ = n₁ + 1; Pfund n₁ = 5.

marking_scheme.step: Levels with energies, gaps shrinking upwards

questions.stem_md: (a) An astronomer records two hydrogen lines from a glowing gas cloud, at 656.3 nm and at 1875 nm. Identify the transition and series of each line. [2] (b) Find the energy, in eV, of a photon of the 1875 nm line. [1] (c) A student says that the two lines cannot come from the same gas, because one is visible and the other infrared. Evaluate this statement, and explain why the same cloud can also emit a line at 102.6 nm. [2] (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, hc = 1240 eV nm)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 656.3 nm: $\dfrac{1}{R\lambda} = 0.139 = \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}$: jump 3 → 2, **Balmer** (visible, red). 1875 nm: $\dfrac{1}{R\lambda} = 0.0486 = \dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{16}$: jump 4 → 3, **Paschen** (infrared).

(b) $E = \dfrac{1240}{1875} = 0.661$ eV $\left(= 13.6\left(\dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{16}\right)\right)$.

(c) The statement is wrong. Both lines come from jumps between energy levels of the same hydrogen atom; the region depends only on the size of the energy gap. An atom excited to n = 4 can fall 4 → 3 (infrared) and then 3 → 2 (red). The line at 102.6 nm is the jump 3 → 1 (Lyman, ultraviolet), another route down from the same level.

questions.solution_md: Identify by 1/(Rλ); E = hc/λ; all lines from one atom’s levels.

marking_scheme.step: Statement wrong: region depends on the gap; same atom

questions.stem_md: A hydrogen atom emits a photon of wavelength 397.0 nm as its electron falls to the n = 2 level. From which level did the electron fall? Give n. (E₁ = −13.6 eV, hc = 1240 eV nm)
questions.solution_md: Photon energy $= \dfrac{1240}{397.0} = 3.123$ eV. Upper level: $E = E_2 + 3.123 = -3.40 + 3.123 = -0.277$ eV $= -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$, so $n^2 = 49.2$ and $n = 7$ (a Balmer line just inside the ultraviolet).

questions.stem_md: The shortest wavelength that hydrogen atoms can emit in the Paschen series is about

options.text_md: 365 nm
820 nm

questions.solution_md: The shortest line is the series limit, $n_2 = \infty$: $\lambda = \dfrac{9}{R} = 820.4$ nm — option (c). 1875 nm is the longest Paschen line; 365 nm is the Balmer limit and 1459 nm the Brackett limit.

questions.stem_md: All the spectral lines of hydrogen produced by electrons falling to the n = 5 level belong to the

options.text_md: Pfund series, in the far infrared
Brackett series, in the infrared
Paschen series, in the infrared
Balmer series, in the visible region

questions.solution_md: Lines ending on n = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 form the Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series; the Pfund lines (2.28–7.46 μm) are in the far infrared — option (a).
